title: 03. Databases & Data Modeling: Indexing
summary: An index is an auxiliary data structure — typically a B-tree, hash, or bitmap — stored alongside a table that lets the database find rows matching a predicate in O(log N) instead of O(N), trading extra storage and slower…
objectives: How does a B-tree index work, and why is it the default index type?
What is the difference between an index scan and an index-only scan?
Why do indexes slow down writes, and how do you decide how many to have?
When does the optimizer choose a sequential scan over an index scan, and why?

sections.title: Explanation
sections.body:
> **In one line:** An index is an auxiliary data structure — typically a B-tree, hash, or bitmap — stored alongside a table that lets the database find rows matching a predicate in O(log N) instead of O(N), trading extra storage and slower writes for dramatically faster reads.

Without an index, finding rows matching `WHERE user_id = 42` requires a **sequential scan** — reading every page of the table and checking the predicate against each row. For a 100-million-row table on disk, that is tens of seconds per query. An index solves this by storing a sorted copy of one or more columns plus a pointer back to the row's physical location (the heap tuple ID in PostgreSQL, the primary key in InnoDB's clustered index). The dominant index type is the **B-tree** (balanced tree), which keeps entries sorted and supports equality (`=`), range (`<`, `>`, `BETWEEN`), and prefix (`LIKE 'abc%'`) lookups in O(log N) time — typically 3–4 levels deep for a billion rows, meaning 3–4 disk reads to find any value. B-trees also support ordered traversal, so `ORDER BY indexed_column` can be served directly from the index without a separate sort step. **Hash indexes** support only equality (`=`) lookups in O(1) but cannot do ranges or ordering; they're useful for specialized workloads like hash joins and in-memory key-value stores. **Bitmap indexes** represent sets of row IDs as bitmaps and are extremely compact for low-cardinality columns (e.g., `gender`, `status`) — useful in data warehouses but rare in OLTP databases.

The fundamental trade-off of indexing is **read speed vs write speed vs storage**. Every index adds an entry per row, so an INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE that touches an indexed column must update every index on that column — a table with 10 indexes pays 10x the write cost. For an OLTP workload with high write volume (e.g., a metrics table receiving 100k inserts/sec), too many indexes can saturate I/O and slow inserts to a crawl. The rule of thumb is to index the columns used in WHERE, JOIN, and ORDER BY clauses, and to remove indexes that are rarely used — PostgreSQL's `pg_stat_user_indexes` shows the read count per index so you can identify unused ones. Storage cost is significant too: a B-tree index is typically 20–50% the size of the table it indexes, so 10 indexes can double the storage footprint. SSDs have made this less painful than in the spinning-disk era, but storage is still money and indexes still must fit in the buffer pool for good performance.

Real-world: Instagram stores tens of billions of photos, each represented by a row in a `media` table with columns like `id`, `user_id`, `created_at`, `url`, `caption`. The most frequent query is "show me user X's recent photos" — `SELECT * FROM media WHERE user_id = ? ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 20`. Without an index on `user_id`, this query scans billions of rows; with a B-tree index on `user_id` (or, better, a composite index on `(user_id, created_at DESC)`), it becomes 3–4 index reads plus 20 heap fetches — milliseconds instead of minutes. Instagram's actual implementation uses sharded MySQL (each shard holds a range of user IDs) with a `(user_id, created_at)` index on each shard, giving sub-10ms latency for the feed query even at planet scale. The trade-off they accept: every photo upload (INSERT) must update the index, adding microseconds — negligible compared to the photo processing pipeline — but at 100k uploads/sec, the index write cost is non-trivial and is one reason they shard (each shard's index fits in memory). Instagram also uses **index-only scans** extensively: by including `url` and `caption` in the index (`INCLUDE` clause in PostgreSQL, or a covering index), the query can be answered from the index alone without fetching the heap row, halving the I/O.

The **index-only scan** is one of the most important optimizations in modern databases. Normally, an index scan finds the index entry (which gives the row's physical location), then fetches the full row from the heap to read the columns not in the index — two I/Os. An index-only scan avoids the heap fetch when all columns needed by the query are present in the index. PostgreSQL's `INCLUDE` clause and the "visibility map" (which tracks whether all rows on a page are visible to all transactions, so the heap fetch can be skipped for visibility checks) make index-only scans possible without bloating the index. The trade-off is the index is larger (it stores extra columns), but the I/O savings are substantial for hot queries. **Covering indexes** are the same idea applied to a composite index: put all columns the query needs into the index, so the query never touches the heap. This is the standard technique for optimizing the top 10 hot queries in an OLTP system — measure which queries dominate, build covering indexes for them, accept the write-cost trade-off.

Indexes are not free even on reads: a poorly chosen index can be worse than a sequential scan. If a query matches a large fraction of the table (say, 30% of rows), the index scan's random I/O pattern (one heap fetch per matching row) is slower than the sequential scan's sequential I/O pattern. The optimizer's **cost model** estimates this: if the predicate matches fewer than ~5% of rows, an index scan wins; above ~20%, a sequential scan wins; in between, a **bitmap scan** combines the index lookup with batched heap fetches to amortize random I/O. Misestimates here cause bad plans: if the optimizer thinks a predicate matches 1% but it actually matches 50%, it picks an index scan that's 10× slower than a sequential scan. The fix is fresh statistics (`ANALYZE`) or extended statistics on correlated columns. Knowing when an index helps and when it hurts — and reading `EXPLAIN ANALYZE` to verify — is the single most important SQL performance skill.

sections.title: Visual Explanation
sections.body:
### Mermaid Diagram
```mermaid
flowchart TD
    Q["SELECT * FROM media WHERE user_id = 42"] --> Opt{Optimizer}
    Opt -->|no index| SS[Sequential Scan: read all pages]
    Opt -->|index on user_id| IS[Index Scan]
    IS --> BT[B-tree root]
    BT --> L1[Leaf page]
    L1 -->|tuple ID| HP[Heap page: fetch full row]
    HP --> R[result row]
    Opt -->|covering index| IOS[Index-Only Scan]
    IOS --> L1
    L1 -->|all cols in index| R

    SS -.->|"slow: O N, scans 100M rows"| R
    IS -.->|"fast: O log N, 3-4 reads"| R
    IOS -.->|"faster: no heap fetch"| R
```

### ASCII Diagram
```
B-tree index on users.email (sorted, balanced, 3-4 levels for 1B rows)

              [ root: m, t, z ]
             /        |         \
       [ a..m ]    [ n..t ]    [ u..z ]
        /  \         |  \         /  \
      ... leaf pages ...
                       |
                       v
  leaf:  [alan@y.com -> tid=42][amy@x.com -> tid=88][ann@b.com -> tid=5]
   (sorted by email; each entry points to the row's physical location)

Query: SELECT * FROM users WHERE email = 'amy@x.com'
  1. root:    'amy' < 'm'  -> go left to [a..m]
  2. interior: 'amy' < 'n' -> go to leaf containing alan, amy, ann
  3. leaf:    found 'amy@x.com' -> tid=88
  4. heap:    fetch page containing tuple 88 -> return row
  Total: ~4 I/Os (vs 100M for sequential scan)

Index types:
  B-tree    O(log N)   =, <, >, BETWEEN, ORDER BY, LIKE 'abc%'   (default)
  Hash      O(1)       = only                                  (no range/order)
  Bitmap    compact    low-cardinality columns (gender, status)  (OLAP)
  GIN/GIST  inverted   full-text search, JSONB, arrays, geo      (PostgreSQL)

Trade-off: each index = +1 entry per write; 10 indexes -> 10x write cost
           index size ~20-50% of table; must fit in buffer pool for speed
```

### Walkthrough
1. The optimizer chooses between a sequential scan (read every page, apply predicate) and an index scan (traverse B-tree, fetch matching rows) based on the estimated selectivity — index scans win for predicates matching <5% of rows.
2. A B-tree index is a balanced tree: the root and interior pages partition the key space; leaf pages hold sorted (key, tuple-ID) entries. Equality lookups traverse 3–4 levels for billion-row tables; range scans traverse to a leaf then walk sideways.
3. Index-only scans avoid the heap fetch when all needed columns are in the index; covering indexes (via INCLUDE or composite) are the standard optimization for hot queries, trading index size for I/O savings.

sections.title: Code
sections.body:
```python
"""
Indexing demo with sqlite3.

Shows: sequential scan vs index scan (via EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN),
timing difference on a 200k-row table, and a covering-index concept.

Run:  python3 indexing_demo.py
"""

import sqlite3, time, tempfile, os

path = tempfile.mktemp(suffix=".db")
conn = sqlite3.connect(path)
cur = conn.cursor()

# --- schema: photos table mimicking Instagram's media table ---
cur.executescript("""
CREATE TABLE photos (
    id        INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
    user_id   INTEGER NOT NULL,
    created_at INTEGER NOT NULL,
    url       TEXT NOT NULL,
    caption   TEXT
);
""")

# --- insert 200,000 rows: 10,000 users, ~20 photos each ---
import random
random.seed(0)
now = int(time.time())
rows = []
for i in range(1, 200001):
    uid = (i % 10000) + 1
    rows.append((i, uid, now - random.randint(0, 86400 * 365),
                 f"https://cdn/img/{i}.jpg", f"caption {i}"))
cur.executemany("INSERT INTO photos VALUES (?,?,?,?,?)", rows)
conn.commit()
print(f"inserted {cur.execute('SELECT COUNT(*) FROM photos').fetchone()[0]} rows")

# --- without index: sequential scan ---
print("\n-- EXPLAIN without index (sequential scan expected) --")
for r in cur.execute("EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN SELECT url FROM photos WHERE user_id = 42"):
    print(" ", r)

def time_query(sql):
    t0 = time.perf_counter()
    rows = cur.execute(sql).fetchall()
    return (time.perf_counter() - t0) * 1000, len(rows)

ms, n = time_query("SELECT url FROM photos WHERE user_id = 42")
print(f"  query without index: {ms:.2f} ms, {n} rows")

# --- add a B-tree index on user_id ---
cur.execute("CREATE INDEX idx_photos_user_id ON photos(user_id)")
conn.commit()

print("\n-- EXPLAIN with index on user_id (index scan expected) --")
for r in cur.execute("EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN SELECT url FROM photos WHERE user_id = 42"):
    print(" ", r)

ms, n = time_query("SELECT url FROM photos WHERE user_id = 42")
print(f"  query WITH index:    {ms:.2f} ms, {n} rows  (massive speedup)")

# --- composite covering index: (user_id, created_at) INCLUDE (url) ---
# sqlite doesn't support INCLUDE; emulate with composite (user_id, created_at, url)
cur.execute("CREATE INDEX idx_photos_covering ON photos(user_id, created_at, url)")
conn.commit()

print("\n-- EXPLAIN with covering composite index (index-only scan expected) --")
for r in cur.execute(
    "EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN SELECT url FROM photos WHERE user_id = 42 ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 20"
):
    print(" ", r)

ms, n = time_query(
    "SELECT url FROM photos WHERE user_id = 42 ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 20"
)
print(f"  feed query (covering): {ms:.2f} ms, {n} rows")

# --- range query: another win for B-tree ---
print("\n-- EXPLAIN range query (BETWEEN) --")
for r in cur.execute(
    "EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN SELECT COUNT(*) FROM photos WHERE user_id BETWEEN 100 AND 200"
):
    print(" ", r)

# --- write-cost demonstration: timing an INSERT with vs without many indexes ---
def time_inserts(n=1000):
    t0 = time.perf_counter()
    cur.executemany(
        "INSERT INTO photos(id, user_id, created_at, url, caption) VALUES (?,?,?,?,?)",
        [(10_000_000 + i, 999, now, f"u{i}", "c") for i in range(n)],
    )
    conn.commit()
    return (time.perf_counter() - t0) * 1000

ms_with = time_inserts(1000)
print(f"\n-- INSERT 1000 rows with 2 indexes: {ms_with:.2f} ms")

# Drop indexes, time the same inserts
cur.execute("DROP INDEX idx_photos_user_id")
cur.execute("DROP INDEX idx_photos_covering")
conn.commit()
ms_without = time_inserts(1000)
print(f"   INSERT 1000 rows with NO indexes: {ms_without:.2f} ms  (writes faster without indexes)")

conn.close()
os.unlink(path)
```

quiz.question: How does a B-tree index work, and why is it the default index type?
options: Most likely a statistics issue: the optimizer estimates the predicate matches too many rows (e.g., >20%) and picks a sequential scan instead.
The optimal index is a composite covering index on (user_id, created_at DESC) INCLUDE (url, caption) (PostgreSQL syntax) or (user_id, created_at, url, caption) as a…
Two reasonable options: (a) a composite index on (customer_id, status) — optimal for this exact query, also useful for WHERE customer_id = ? alone (leftmost prefix).
A B-tree (balanced tree) is a sorted, multi-level tree where every leaf is at the same depth.
quiz.explanation: A B-tree (balanced tree) is a sorted, multi-level tree where every leaf is at the same depth. The root and interior pages contain key values that partition the key space — e.g., a root with keys [m, t, z] routes lookups for amy to the leftmost child, paul to the middle, xavier to the right.

options: A partial index is an index that covers only rows matching a WHERE clause — e.g., CREATE INDEX idx_unpaid_orders ON orders(user_id) WHERE status = 'unpaid'.

An index-only scan answers the query entirely from the index, with no heap fetch — possible only when every column the query needs (in SELECT, WHERE, ORDER BY) is present in the index.
quiz.explanation: index scan** uses the index to find matching tuple IDs, then fetches each row from the heap (table storage) to read columns not present in the index. So per matching row: one index page read + one heap page read = two I/Os (potentially random).

options: A partial index is an index that covers only rows matching a WHERE clause — e.g., CREATE INDEX idx_unpaid_orders ON orders(user_id) WHERE status = 'unpaid'.
bitmap scan** is a two-phase index access: first, the index lookup produces a bitmap of tuple IDs matching the predicate (one bit per page, or per tuple, depending on precision); second,…

quiz.explanation: bitmap scan** is a two-phase index access: first, the index lookup produces a bitmap of tuple IDs matching the predicate (one bit per page, or per tuple, depending on precision); second, the heap fetches are done in page-number order, converting random I/O into mostly-sequential I/O. There are two variants: Bitmap Index Scan (builds the bitmap) and Bitmap Heap Scan (fetches the pages in sorted order).
